lesson.title: Genotype and Phenotype: What Is Inherited versus What Is Seen
lesson.summary: Genotype is the specific combination of alleles an organism carries for a gene, while phenotype is the observable trait that results, and because of dominance, different genotypes can produce the exact same phenotype.
lesson.body:
Genotype refers to the actual combination of alleles an organism carries at a given locus, for example PP, Pp, or pp for the flower color gene in peas. Phenotype refers to the observable trait that results from that genotype, for example purple flowers or white flowers. These two ideas are closely related but not the same thing, and the previous chapter on dominant and recessive alleles already showed exactly why they can diverge. Because P is dominant over p, PP and Pp are two different genotypes, yet they produce the same phenotype, purple flowers. Only the pp genotype produces the white phenotype.

It is worth noting, without straying too far from the single-gene traits covered in this unit, that phenotype is not always determined by just one gene acting alone. Many observable traits can be influenced by more than one gene working together, and some traits are also shaped by environmental conditions in addition to genotype. The clean, predictable genotype to phenotype relationships worked out in this unit, following Mendel's own approach, apply most directly to traits controlled by a single gene with straightforward dominance, which is exactly the kind of trait these chapters focus on.

The Pp by Pp cross used throughout the last two chapters illustrates the genotype versus phenotype distinction directly. The genotype ratio among the offspring is 1 PP to 2 Pp to 1 pp, three distinct genotype classes in a 1 to 2 to 1 ratio. The phenotype ratio, by contrast, is 3 purple to 1 white, only two distinct phenotype classes, because the PP and Pp genotype classes both produce the purple phenotype and collapse into one visible category. The genotype ratio and the phenotype ratio are different numbers precisely because genotype and phenotype are different things, and dominance is the reason they diverge here.

To describe an organism's genotype fully and precisely, it also matters whether the two alleles it carries at a locus are the same as each other or different from each other. That distinction has its own vocabulary, homozygous and heterozygous, covered next.
